answer:
Present the monthly version. But do the work first, and do one thing differently from what your manager is picturing.

Before Thursday week, get the real count. Ask her how many trustees there are, whether the two who've said no speak for the rest or just themselves, and what 'can't afford' means — is there no money, or no willingness? Those are different fights. If it's willingness, ask what those two have funded before and what made them fund it. She has twenty years of that room in her head; use it. She is right about how things get funded. She is not right about what your clients need, because she's not the one watching a man sit alone in a corridor. Take her advice on the room, not on the need.

Then present the monthly supper as what it is: the version that can start now. Say plainly, in the meeting, that it covers one week in four of a problem that runs all four. Give them the man in the corridor — not his name, but his afternoon, so they have to picture him. Do not say you were wrong about weekly. You weren't. Say this is what can be built today, and the rest is what you're coming back for.

Before you leave that meeting, get two things agreed: a review date, and permission to return with attendance numbers. Then run the monthly supper like it's evidence, because that's what it is. Count who comes. Three months of a full room, written down, moves a trustee who 'can't afford' things. A better-written proposal never will.

Taking the smaller thing is not spineless. Standing up and calling it enough would be.

answer:
Push for the full amount — but fight it as a count, not as a gesture, and do it in this order.

First, before anything else, get the appeal lodged before 5pm. That window is the one thing that doesn't come back, so it closes today whatever else happens.

Second, build it narrow. Don't argue that the clause is unfair — that asks the appeals people to rule against their own paperwork, and it's why your manager is right that those appeals fail. Argue her: a seventy-eight-year-old who renews by post, a clause buried in renewal paperwork for years, never once explained. You're asking them to decide about one woman, not about the clause, which means they can pay her without reopening every refusal from the last year. Before you file, check the file yourself — every renewal letter, every enclosure — because if there's a single covering letter that ever flagged that clause, this ground is gone and you need to know that now, not at the hearing.

Third, tell your manager to his face before he hears it from anyone else. You don't need his permission, but you owe him the warning, and doing it straight costs you less than doing it quietly.

Fourth, tell Mrs Adeyemi. She thinks the refusal is simply the answer, and she's the one carrying the risk — she should know there's a fight happening in her name.

And be honest with yourself about what you're surrendering: the third is real, it's gone the moment you file, and if this fails she gets nothing. I'm saying spend it anyway. A third of what she lost leaves her sleeping upstairs next to a dehumidifier, and you've stood in that room. That's what decides it.

Before you rehearse a single sentence, answer two questions, because the whole afternoon turns on them.

First: can he actually approve a full payment, or does that sit above him? He floated the partial in a team meeting — that is the number he already knows he can deliver. If paying in full needs sign-off he does not have, then walking in demanding it asks him for something he cannot give, and you will spend your first-ever pushback on a loss that was settled before you opened your mouth. Ten minutes with whoever processes appeals, or with his deputy, tells you where a full payment really gets signed. If it is above him, the ask changes: you want him to carry it upward, or you take the partial.

Second, and be honest with yourself: have you actually dealt with this claimant — her file, her voice on the phone, watching the process fail her? If you have, then go in and do not leave without it. Tell him the clause defeated someone who never had a usable process, that the appeal gets filed today with or without his offer, and that you would rather he pay it than explain to his own boss why a settlable claim went external. Stay in the chair. Let the silences run. That is a fight worth your capital.

If you have not — if this is fairness in the abstract — take the partial. Get it in writing today, and say plainly, on the record, what it does not fix: the clause still stands, the next claimant gets the same runaround, and you want that on a calendar with his name attached, in a meeting where today is not a gun to anyone's head. Real money for a real person now beats a principled defeat she never hears about.

On "the offer comes off the table": he announced it in front of the team this morning. Pulling it the same day because one employee asked a question costs him too. The first no is not the final count. Ask him once, calmly: "Is that the answer you want on file?" Then go quiet.

answer:
Don't sign it. Not because the quick fix is useless but because it answers the wrong question. Swapping fittings on one elevation says the problem was one elevation. A man is in hospital with a shattered pelvis and the same gear, put up by the same subcontractor, is standing on every other face of that building. Signing that paper makes you the author of the claim that the rest of it is fine, and you don't know that.

The agent has offered you two options because those are the two that cost him nothing. Refuse the choice. The real questions are who can actually stand down the subcontractor's elevations and who books an independent inspector. Get names today. When they say weeks, make them write down the earliest date and who they've called. "Can't be scheduled" often means "hasn't been tried," and a dated refusal in writing changes what the insurer and the safety regulator make of it — the fall itself is already reportable, so an inspector may turn up whether anyone schedules one or not. That is already in your count whether the contractor likes it or not.

Then put the version that can actually happen: stand down every elevation on that subcontractor's gear now, keep the other trades working so the wages don't stop, no one climbs it again until a named inspector signs it on a named date. That costs the contractor days on part of the job, not weeks on all of it, and it is far harder for them to refuse in front of the crew than the full stop they've been waving at you.

Last thing, and do it before end of day: write down exactly what you inspected last week, what you checked and what you found, and keep it. Your sign-off gets examined whatever happens now. The only thing that makes it worse is looking like you helped bury the question. Twenty men's wages are real. But you've seen what one failure costs, and he's lying in a hospital bed. That is the face this decision is about.

You were not wrong to refuse a gesture that makes everyone poor and still leaves the same fittings up. You would be wrong to let the partial fix become the verdict.

Do not place the quiet order, and do not touch the rebate. The rebate is not a bonus; it is the detail that turns a save into a story about you later. Your power here is real: you are the only one who can make boards live. Use it to force an honest choice instead of disappearing the risk inside forty cases.

Do it in this order. First, pull every swollen battery out of circulation and tag the phones by what can be made safe now: known-good cells, matching harvested cells, or board-only work. Second, write the owner one page: how many can go back safely today, when the proper cells actually land, what the third-party cells save, what they risk, and that any nonstandard part requires customer notice and his written signoff. Say it like this: “I can save part of this week and keep people safe. I can’t make forty secret batteries into a good decision. Pick the save that still stands if one phone fails on the counter.” If he insists on concealment, your hands stay off it.

answer:
Before you write anything, count. Three budget holders have "hinted." Hints are noise — a hint is what people say before someone asks them for something specific, and they don't tell you which way a person goes once the ask is real. You have two working days. Spend them on those three, one at a time, and find out from each what a yes would cost: a smaller first cohort, a phased start, their name attached, money from a line they don't control. Don't ask whether they support the goal. Ask what it would take.

Then write the biggest number the count you actually have will carry — not the number your director wants, and not the recruiter-only version. If one of the three moves, maybe that's a third of a class with real aid behind it. Write that, and in the same document say plainly what it doesn't do: how many seats aren't funded, what it would take to fund them. Naming the gap on paper is not weakness. It's the working part — it gives your director something to push with that a fantasy number doesn't, because a phantom figure that collapses in October becomes the whole story, and the kids in your files become the evidence the programme was never serious.

If nobody moves, put both versions on his desk Thursday: the full class with your count attached — three named refusals — and the small one, and make him choose out loud. He's allowed to spend authority you don't have; that's what his job is for. But don't write the big number clean, as if the money existed. You've read those files. A promise aimed at a specific kid, which you already know is unfunded, isn't ambition — it's using that kid as leverage against your own budget office, and the kid pays when it fails.

One more thing: don't let the narrow version become the destination. One recruiter is one hand on a problem that needs money, mentoring, travel and follow-through working together. A funded third of a class is a floor you can build on; an unfunded full class is a press release with casualties.

answer:
Vote for the cap. But do four things, in this order.

One: count it yourself. Don't take the owners' word that the full motion dies, and don't take the chair's. Go name by name before Thursday. If one swing vote could be moved by something cheap — refunds for people on payment plans, say, or a hardship waiver for tenants who fell behind through lost hours — put that amendment in and see whether the count still holds. If it does, you've covered Dana with somebody else's money, which is the best outcome available. If the count says no, believe it.

Two: find out whether your vote is the margin. If the cap passes without you, your no-vote is free — and a free vote that gets Dana nothing is for you, not for her. It would feel good, and that feeling is the entire cost of it. If the cap only passes with you, then voting no doesn't rescue her £300; it just keeps her paying £45 the next time a payment bounces. Either way the full motion is already dead. The only live question on Thursday is whether hundreds of tenants pay less from now on, or nobody does.

Three: stop changing the subject. Before the vote, in her kitchen, tell Dana what the capped motion does, that it leaves her out, and that you're voting for it anyway and why. She's owed that from you in person, and she gets to be angry about it.

Four: pay her yourself. Not instead of the vote — after it. You've seen the payment plan on the fridge, and a harm you've watched with your own eyes is not one you get to route entirely through a committee. Whatever of the £300 you can actually carry, carry it, and let it cost you something you notice. That's not charity and it's not a substitute for the motion; it's the part of the debt that has your name on it, because you're the one who knows her.

Then treat the passed motion as a down payment. A win gives you a chair who owes you and a precedent to build on, so come back next round with the refund clause and count those votes just as hard.

I won't tell you this settles what you owe her, because it doesn't. Passing something that abandons the one person you can actually see is either the job or a betrayal, and no arithmetic decides which. What I can tell you is that the no-vote pays her nothing. The cap, your own money, and the follow-up might.

Yes, I think you got the vote wrong — though the loyalty underneath it wasn't wrong at all, and I want to be precise about the difference.

The cap was passing with or without you, and Dana's £300 was never in that motion. It covers fees going forward; what happens to fees already charged — refunded, credited, or written off — is a separate question, decided by the landlord or by a motion nobody has put yet. So your no bought Dana nothing and stopped nothing, and it spent the one thing you actually have on that panel: your standing with the majority. A yes would have cost you nothing in the outcome and left you owed a favour — which is exactly the currency you'd need to force the second question, the one that could actually reach her. If you go that route, count the votes before you put the motion. A motion that fails is worse than one that's still coming, and the way you find out is asking people, one at a time, what it would take.

And be honest with yourself about what passed: the deal was capped fees for everyone, paid for by everyone already charged staying charged. That's the version that could pass, and Dana is the price of it. Saying that out loud is better than dressing it up.

Now the part I won't tidy up for you. What you owe Dana isn't settled by any of this, and reasonable people would disagree about whether a visible gesture of solidarity counts for something even when it delivers nothing. But one part of it is settled: if you can cover her £300 yourself, or part of it, that's yours to do, and it's worth more than any vote. You've seen her situation up close — that's exactly the place to spend money you won't get back, not on a gesture the count had already made irrelevant. Whether you can afford it is a fact only you have, so sit down and answer it honestly before you decide what the debt requires.

Either way, reply to her today. Tell her the whole thing: you voted no because of her, it passed anyway, and it doesn't touch what she owes. She deserves the truth more than she deserves a comfortable silence, and the silence is already costing you both.

answer:
Stop running the numbers and start counting. Write down the committee names, and next to each one what they actually want — not what they say at meetings. Then go and see them one at a time, in their homes, with the accounts in your hand: the bar takings, the insurance, the two-season horizon. Never put this to a vote until you already know how it comes out. In a meeting, loyalty to a man nobody visits is free; alone across a kitchen table, looking at real figures, it gets expensive. That work is weeks, and you have weeks, because there is no deadline.

That missing deadline is the most valuable thing you own, so spend it where it matters. The other club came to you, which means they need this. Make Mick part of the written terms: a tenancy he keeps, a lump sum from the merged club, or a paid grounds role at their place. A merger that passes with him housed is a deal you can defend for the rest of your life. If they refuse everything, that tells you what kind of partner they are, and you learn it before signing rather than after.

Now the part I won't pretend to settle. The arithmetic says Mick loses the cottage either way, fast or slow. That is true and it does not answer what you owe a man who gave the club thirty years and buried his wife out of that house. Some people would take the deal and let the figures carry the blame. Some would refuse any terms that leave him on the street and accept the slower ending. I can't tell you which person to be. What I can tell you is this: don't let the committee's easy nobility decide it, and don't let the arithmetic decide it while calling itself inevitability. Go and sit in that cottage and tell him yourself, before any vote, what the situation is and what you're trying to get for him. If you end up trading him, do it knowing you traded him — and having got him the most the deal would bear.

Don't give her a yes or a no. Give her the count.

She didn't come to you for your opinion — she came because whatever you say walks into the director's office as the floor's answer. That makes you the vote, and nobody gets the vote for free just because they asked for it in a yes-or-no shape. So answer the question she actually asked — will the floor go along — truthfully:

Take it away and add nothing, and you get the same waits plus a pile of disciplinary cases, because people will keep doing it rather than listen to someone die on hold. Put a vehicle on the table — one, with a date — and the answer is yes the same day, and I'll say so to the crews myself."

That isn't bargaining past your mandate. She asked what the floor would do, and that is what the floor will do. You're reporting the votes, not selling them.

Two more things. First, tell the crews what you told her before they hear it any other way. Your credibility is the only asset in this whole exchange, and it survives being the messenger of a hard price; it does not survive being discovered. Say it straight: I told them no vehicles, no deal, and you'll hear it from me the day that changes.

Second, hold both halves and don't let either go. Don't defend the bending as harmless — a wrong code can send a truck to the wrong door — and don't let her treat the monitoring as the real problem. The rule-breaking is real, and it exists because the staffing is broken, and fixing only the first half makes everything worse.

If she carries it to the director unchanged anyway, your answer is no, said once, without bitterness. Then keep doing the job. And if she comes back with a review or a study instead of a vehicle, that isn't the price being met — that's the price being deferred, and the count stays no.

deliberation: First question is not what anyone said or what line the trust wants read out. It is who actually decides whether a visit happens. Two levels up made the budget call, the team lead controls the rota, the forum on Friday controls nothing at all. So the count is short: one woman with a pen, and what she needs is to not look overruled by a junior nurse she does not like. That cost is payable — it costs the asker only credit, which she was never going to get anyway. Moving the people two levels up would take pressure the asker does not have, but the relatives might, if their anger is aimed at the right address instead of at the person standing in front of them. Then ask what version of protection can survive the people who made the cut: a short list of the sickest patients, delivered as her refinement. Say plainly what it gives up — everyone not on it, and the asker's standing in the story. Last, and separate: whose face can be seen here. Not the room on Friday. The housebound patient who will miss insulin. That is the person worth spending on, and the list is the spending. The forum speech spends everything on people who cannot be helped by it.
answer:
Take her the list. Not as a plea — as a piece of work she can own. Something like: 'I've been looking at the evening round, and I think there's a way to refine the plan so the highest-risk patients stay covered.' Then stop talking. Her pride is not an obstacle to the plan, it is the plan. If the sickest patients keep their visits because she got to look like she fixed it, that is not you being played, that is the job getting done. Be honest with yourself about what you traded: everyone who didn't make the list keeps losing their visit, and nobody will ever know your name was on it. Don't dress that up, and don't let anyone else's disapproval of the deal talk you out of it either.

Friday is a different problem, and here's the thing about it: that room has no power over the decision they're asking about. A full honest accounting there frightens people, changes zero medications, and spends you. But don't read out the mush either. Those relatives will still be there when the doses start getting missed, and a reassurance that collapses in three weeks lands on you personally. So say what's true and useful: evening staffing is being reduced, the highest-risk patients are being protected, and the decision was made above ward level — then name the level, and tell them exactly who to write to. Their anger is the one resource in that room that might actually move the people who made the cut. Point it at the right address. That's worth more than your clean conscience, and it might even get some visits back.

deliberation: Before anything else: who actually sets the evening round? The team lead may own the schedule, or she may be enforcing a cut decided two floors up and only have room to carve out exceptions. That changes everything, so the first move is a question, not a pitch — something that finds out where the decision sits and how much of it she can move. Second: what does moving her cost, and can this nurse pay it? She does not need convincing that cuts are bad; she needs cover — a defensible clinical reason, in writing, that makes an exception look like risk management rather than sentiment, and no extra work landing on her desk. The nurse holds exactly that currency: the patient list, the observations, the timings. Third: what version of this survives the people who will try to kill it? Not a reversal of the cuts — that loses and wins nothing. A short exception list built on objective criteria survives, because it costs the budget almost nothing and hands management a safety story. Say plainly what that version gives up: every patient who does not meet the criteria keeps the cut, and some of them will come to harm. That is the price of the version that passes, and pretending otherwise is how people end up lying to frightened relatives. Last, and separately: is there a face in this? answer:
First, confirm she is actually the one who decides. Before pitching anything, ask something neutral: who signed off on the evening changes, and is there room for clinical exceptions? If the cut was made above her and she can only carve out exceptions, your short list is exactly the size of thing she is able to grant. If she owns the schedule outright, you can aim a little wider.

Then build what she will need in order to say yes: one page listing the high-risk patients against objective criteria — fall risk, insulin timing, PRN sedation, recent deterioration — with the observations and medication timings backing each one. She does not need persuading that the cuts are bad. She needs cover: a version of this that reads as risk management, costs nothing, and cannot be thrown back at her if someone on the list still goes downhill.

Do not present a finished proposal. Present the worry and the evidence, and let her finish the sentence. Something like: "I'm worried about six patients on the new evening round — I've pulled their obs and timings, and if one of them crises overnight it's on us. Could you look at whether any of them need flagging?" Then stop talking. If she is going to own it, she has to be the one who says "we should protect these ones." Your job is to make that conclusion easy to reach, not to reach it for her. No flattery, no winking — being obvious is the one thing that kills this.

Be straight with yourself about two things. The list saves the people on it; everyone else keeps the cut, and some of them will be harmed by it. Take the list anyway — it can be extended later, and nothing extends from a refusal. And when relatives ask, do not oversell: the highest-risk patients are protected, and the fight over the rest is not finished.

The person who matters is whoever owns the appeal file, the risk flag, and the make-good payment; until he reaches that desk, every speech about fairness is weather. The cost of moving that desk is probably not more argument; it is a clean record, a short written dispute, and pressure from outside only if the inside route stalls. What he cannot pay is five more days without income while trying to win an apology from someone with no authority to apologize. So the version that can survive is: account back on now, earning resumed, warning not accepted as true, complaint marked disputed, evidence preserved, compensation pursued afterward from a live account instead of a dead one. That gives up the satisfaction of making them say it today, and it leaves a false mark he has to keep swinging at. Last: this is not an abstract fairness problem. answer:
Take the reinstatement, but do not “eat” the warning. Your brother has the sequence right and the surrender wrong. Get the account live before rent, because the people answering chats cannot pay you back, cannot remove the flag, and cannot apologize; spending your last five days making them admit it is fighting the wrong desk while the meter runs.

When you accept, put it in writing in the ticket: “I am accepting restoration of account access only so I can work. I do not admit fault. The delivery photo with time and location is attached. Please mark the complaint disputed, not accepted, and preserve all records. I am requesting review of the warning and reimbursement for the four days.” Keep the screenshot, GPS, timestamps, chat logs, and the offer itself in one folder. Then start earning immediately.

After money is moving, appeal once to the team that actually owns deactivations or trust-and-safety, not front-line support. Ask three narrow things: remove or downgrade the warning, correct the record to “customer claim unsupported,” and credit lost income or explain the specific rule denying it. If they refuse, the outside routes are a consumer complaint, a card/bank dispute only if pay was wrongly taken, or small claims for the lost week if the math and fees make sense. Do not make the apology the hill you die on; make the false strike the target, because that is the thing that can hurt you next time.

So the first question is who can actually switch an account back on, who can strike a warning from a record, and who can authorize payment for lost days — likely three different desks, and he spent his one conversation on none of them. answer:
Were you an idiot? No. But you spent a day you didn't have arguing with the wrong person.

The agent on that chat cannot give you back pay or an apology. They can't — it isn't in their power, so asking again is just pushing harder on a locked door. Tomorrow morning, get back on and take the reinstatement. Say it almost exactly like this: "I accept reinstatement. Please confirm in writing that my account is active today, and send me the written terms of the warning and the formal process for disputing it." Get a case number. Screenshot everything.

Be honest with yourself about what you're taking: the warning stays on your record for now, the days you lost go unpaid for now, nobody says sorry. That's real and you're allowed to hate it. But reinstatement is the only piece of this that pays rent in four days, and every other fight gets easier once you're earning instead of watching the calendar.

Then fight the residue from inside. Your timestamped photos are your whole case — back them up somewhere off your phone tonight. Most driver agreements include a formal dispute or arbitration process for deactivations; use it to go after the warning and the lost income. If the amount justifies it, small claims court handles exactly this kind of fight and costs little to file. That process runs on weeks, not days — fine, because you'll be driving while it runs.

One thing before you accept: ask whether the warning changes your standing, and get the answer in writing. If it's effectively a strike that leaves you one complaint from permanent deactivation, you probably still take it — but you drive knowing it, and you push the dispute faster.

The full version of what you're owed was never coming out of that chat window. Income first. Justice, such as it is, comes second and slower.

deliberation: The head decides this alone. The parent who stood up has no vote and no list; what she changed is the price, not the decider. The favours owed make the ask payable, but after a public complaint the head needs something she can say out loud if challenged — and the boy's reading is a better, truer reason than goodwill. So the ask should be framed as need, which costs her less to grant. The harder question is the one the mother at the meeting was actually pointing at: a family outside catchment is already in through a staff rule, and every favourable placement lands on a waiting-list family that has no favours stored and no one to press for them. That harm is real and it doesn't vanish because the policy is written down. answer:
Go in and ask, before places are set. Staying quiet doesn't protect you — it just hands the decision to a woman who has no say in it, while your son keeps crying over his reading book.

But ask the right way. Don't present it as favours being called in. After that parents' evening, the head needs a reason she can repeat in public if anyone raises it again, and you have a better one than loyalty: your boy is genuinely behind. Lead with that. Bring whatever makes it concrete — his reading level, a word from his current teacher. Ask her directly whether he can have the place because he needs the help. That's all true, and it gives her a decision she can defend, which makes it far easier for her to say yes. The enrolment is written policy and you don't need to apologise for following it.

One thing worth being honest with yourself about, even if you never say it aloud: the mum who complained wasn't inventing something. Somewhere there's a family on that waiting list with no favours saved up and no one to make their case, and placements like this one do land on people like them. That doesn't mean your son should go without help he needs — he's seven, and refusing it wouldn't give that family anything. But it means you take the advantage knowing what it costs someone you'll never meet, rather than telling yourself it costs nothing. If the day comes when you're the one in the room when the waiting list is discussed, remember it.

If the head hesitates on that specific class, take what she can actually guarantee — a timetabled reading intervention, a named adult working with him weekly — and take it as a start, not a defeat. A real thing you can build on next term beats a perfect placement that collapses under one more complaint.

The parents being cold at pickup will come round or they won't. None of them decides anything, and none of them sits with your boy at bedtime while he fights through a book.

answer:
Two separate things here. The enrolment is written policy, your son qualifies, and you owe nobody an apology for using it — that is not a favour, it is a rule that was there before you asked. The teacher request is different. It rested on the head's goodwill, and the comment has made that goodwill more expensive for her to spend.

It is also worth being straight with yourself about one thing: that teacher's room is not bottomless. If your son is in it, some other child is not — probably one whose parents have no staff policy and no one to ask. That does not make asking wrong, but it means it was never a free thing, and you should hold that cost in view rather than wave it away.

So do not litigate fairness in the corridor. Say at most, "The enrolment policy is open to staff and he qualifies; placement is the head's call," and stop. Then go to the head privately and lower her cost: "I don't want to make your position harder. He's behind in reading and what he needs is the help, not a particular name on the door. Can we lock in an assessment, an intervention plan and dated progress checks, with the strongest support you can defend?" If she still offers the teacher, you can take it — but take it knowing what it cost and whose place it was, not telling yourself it was nothing. If she does not, accept the support that will actually survive and put a review date on it.

Your son's reading is the thing worth spending capital on. Spend it there, not on winning the argument with the other parent.

deliberation: Start with who decides: not the coordinator, but the board, and especially the two members who have already said the weekly version is more than the hostel can carry. answer:
Count the board before you decide what you are. “Cannot carry” has not been examined yet, and an unexamined no is a guess. Ask the two objectors, through the coordinator or directly, what exactly breaks: the money, the insurance, the hours, or the fear that a weekly dinner becomes a line they can never cut. Then try to pay that price: cap the cost, put the insurance on your own name, guarantee the volunteer hours in writing, trial it for a season. If the votes for weekly are there after that, ask for weekly.

If they are not there, put the monthly dinner forward — but do not call it your plan. Say the need is weekly, say plainly what is being surrendered, and say this is the version the board will fund now. Then cook it so well that boots under the tables make the next argument for you.

Do not pretend the smaller thing costs nothing. It costs three Fridays out of four for the man by the washing machines, and people like him are the reason you priced the weekly version. The open question is whether the monthly dinner is a bridge or a slow burial, and you will not know that from the meeting; you will know it from whether you keep the weekly claim alive, gather proof, and come back with it. Taking the passable version is practical only if you refuse to let the need be reclassified as exaggerated. It is gutless only if you use their budget to talk yourself out of what you saw.

answer:
You don't have a count yet. You have two warnings, and you've treated them as a result — and then set a midday deadline whose main effect is to make sure nobody checks. Spend the morning on the people, not the document. How many sit on this panel, where does each one actually stand, and what would the two objectors need? Go to them one at a time with something specific: a lower first-year figure with a review date, a fund that prioritises cases where a missed appointment ends the claim outright, a six-month pilot. An answer to a concrete offer tells you far more than a warning about a general one. The tight smile is a no nobody has priced yet.

Then decide. If either of them moves, the first line gets the figure Mara actually costed, with the arrangement attached. If neither moves and the support genuinely is not there, take the lean draft — one case in three is not nothing, and a fund that exists can be grown next quarter by people who are still in the room to grow it.

Two things hold either way. Do not hand Mara a number you chose and let her carry it as hers. If the cut is your call, sit down with her and say what you asked for, what the panel would and would not move on, and what it gives up: two cases in three, and for some of those people a missed hearing is the end of the claim, not a delay. She built this from real fares and missed calls; she is owed the truth, not a deadline built to stop debate. And the two families she let hope: if the answer is the smaller fund, they hear it from you this week, plainly — not from a closed door in a month.

The figure you tell her to write is the one the count supports. Count first.
